lead: Two stories about who receives God’s gift. In the First Reading, an enemy general with a skin disease is healed in the Jordan, once he stops demanding a cure fit for his rank. In the Gospel, Jesus reminds his own townspeople of that same general, and they try to kill him for it. Between the two the Psalm sings of a soul that thirsts for the living God. Thirst is the one qualification. The key words are wash, clean and accepted.

set: Elisha worked in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC, when Israel and Aram (Syria, with its capital at Damascus) were often at war. The first verse holds a surprise: it was “the Lord” who had given victory to Aram. The God of Israel is at work in the career of Israel’s enemy before that enemy has ever heard of him.

Naaman has rank, wealth and the favor of his king, and he has a disease that none of it can touch. The Hebrew word translated “leprosy” covers a range of skin conditions, and not only what we now call Hansen’s disease. The reading ends in the middle of v. 15, with Naaman’s confession of faith.
str: vv. 1–3: the great man and the captive girl who knows where help is.
vv. 4–7: the wrong road: king writes to king, and the king of Israel panics.
vv. 8–10: Elisha sends a message and does not come out.
vv. 11–12: Naaman’s anger: too plain, and the wrong river.
vv. 13–14: his servants reason with him; he goes down and is healed.
v. 15: he returns and confesses the one God.
kw: A general word for serious skin diseases. Here it stands for what lies beyond all human power: the king of Israel himself says that only God could cure it (5:7).

The story begins with a “little girl”, a captive who serves in Naaman’s house (5:2), and it ends with the proud commander’s flesh made like that of a “little boy” (5:14). The two Hebrew phrases match. He is healed by becoming small.
The word comes four times (5:10, 12, 13, 14). Naaman comes asking for a cure; what he receives is called cleansing, and a word of worship comes with it.
vv: If only my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria!
She has been carried off from her home and she has no name in the story. She could have enjoyed her master’s misfortune. Her one sentence starts the healing of a Gentile commander.
I thought that for me he would surely come out,
“For me.” Naaman has already written the script: a prophet at the door, a solemn prayer, a wave of the hand. What offends him is that God’s way asks nothing grand of him.
So he went down and immersed himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God; his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.

The Greek Old Testament translates “immersed himself” with the verb ebaptisato, the word that gives us baptism. Seven is the number of completeness: he obeys fully, and the waters heal because of the word he obeys.
Now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel;
This is the real goal of the story. He came for his skin and he goes home with faith. In the verses that follow he will say that he will sacrifice to no other god (5:17).
ch: St Ambrose, instructing the newly baptized in his work On the Mysteries, uses Naaman to teach that the water of the font does not heal by itself, and that it is the grace of Christ that heals (in substance). Lent is the season of preparing for that font and of renewing our baptism, and the story speaks to both. Each of us at some point has to go down, drop the script and do the plain thing God asks: go to Confession, make the apology, kneel down to pray.

r.h: No prophet is accepted in his hometown
set: We are in the synagogue at Nazareth, on the Sabbath. Jesus has read from Isaiah 61, announced that the Scripture is fulfilled, and at first “all spoke well of him” (4:22). Then they ask for the wonders he worked at Capernaum (4:23). Mark and Matthew tell of the visit to Nazareth later on. Luke places it at the opening of the ministry, and many scholars think he does so on purpose, as a preview of all that will follow in his Gospel and in Acts.

Jesus is a Jew in his own synagogue, arguing from the Scriptures of Israel. The anger is that of one village on one day, as Luke tells it, and it is no ground for any blame of the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Elijah and Elisha, whom Jesus names, are Israel’s own prophets.
str: vv. 25–26: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath.
vv. 28–29: rage, and the brow of the hill.
v. 30: he goes on his way.
kw: A small word with a sting. A few verses earlier Jesus read of “the year of the Lord’s favor” (4:19), using the same Greek word. The year is dektos and the prophet who brings it is not.
A Phoenician region beyond Israel’s borders. Elijah was sent there in a famine, to a foreign widow (1 Kings 17:9), who fed him and whose son he raised.
The verb at the end of v. 30. Luke uses it again and again for the journey that leads to Jerusalem: “I must be on my way” (13:33).
vv: Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in the prophet’s hometown.
The people want the benefits without the prophet. Being close to Jesus, in a family or a parish or a Christian culture, carries its own danger: we may think we already know him.
There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

Jesus is not saying that God had abandoned Israel. He is answering a claim on his gifts, and in the very next verses he heals many in Capernaum (4:31–41). God’s gift is a gift, and no one has it by right, whether by nation or by neighborhood.
But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.

Luke does not explain how. The hill at Nazareth is not the hour. The rejection and the walking on both point ahead to Jerusalem, where he will again be taken outside the city, and where his way will not end in death.
ch: The Catechism says that the Kingdom was first announced to the children of Israel and is intended for people of all nations (CCC 543). This Gospel holds both halves of that sentence. For us who are Gentiles by descent, it is a matter for gratitude: we are the household of the widow of Zarephath and the company of Naaman. And it is a warning against thinking that we have earned the place.

qa: Why does Jesus seem to provoke his own people?

The people of Nazareth have asked for signs, and he answers with a word that tests what they are asking for. A prophet tells the truth to those he loves, as Elijah and Elisha did. Luke shows that Jesus knew where this would lead, and he went on all the same. The sharpness serves love, and the rest of the Gospel shows him healing, teaching and weeping over his own people (19:41).
study: Where am I like Naaman, wanting God to deal with me in a way that suits my position? What plain thing is God asking of me that I keep putting off?
Who is the “little girl” in my life, the person I overlook, through whom God may be pointing me to help?
